facts: HM Land Registry INSPIRE Index Polygons data published on 5 July 2026 is available by local authority.
New INSPIRE polygon files are published on the first Sunday of each month.
The dataset contains locations of freehold registered property in England and Wales.
The dataset is a subset of HM Land Registry's Index Polygons database.
INSPIRE polygon files are distributed separately for each local authority area.
A polygon crossing a local-authority boundary may occur in both local-authority files.
The current data is downloadable as GML for GIS use.
The dataset is available for reuse under the Open Government Licence subject to its conditions.
Each polygon can be associated with a Land Registry-INSPIRE identifier that relates to a registered title.
guards: Deduplicate cross-local-authority copies before counting candidate geometries.
Record publication month and source local-authority file for every candidate geometry.
Do not treat this freehold-only subset as a complete inventory of all tenure types.

facts: INSPIRE polygons show the position and indicative extent of a registered property.
The extent of land in a registered title cannot be established from INSPIRE Index Polygons.
HM Land Registry directs users to the individual title plan to identify the registered title extent.
Each INSPIRE polygon has a unique Land Registry-INSPIRE ID.
A registered title can contain several separate polygons, each with its own INSPIRE ID.
Absence of an INSPIRE ID can mean land is unregistered, leasehold, or another tenure not present in the dataset.
The service describes INSPIRE as an open-source dataset for registered freehold property.
The dataset is updated monthly and reflects data from the previous month.
INSPIRE IDs can be used with HM Land Registry property services to locate the related title registration and plan.
guards: Never promote an INSPIRE polygon alone as an exact legal boundary.
Keep INSPIRE candidate geometry evidence separate from title-plan and determined-boundary evidence classes.
Do not infer that a property is unregistered solely because no INSPIRE polygon is found.

facts: HM Land Registry INSPIRE polygon geometry is captured against the British National Grid.
Polygon points are represented by X and Y values referencing British National Grid positions.
British National Grid is identified in the guidance as EPSG:27700.
INSPIRE GML can be converted in GIS software to formats including GeoJSON, KML, DXF and shapefile.
GIS software can re-project the data to other coordinate reference systems.
The guidance gives EPSG:3857 as an example projection used by common web mapping tools.
Coordinate conversion calculations can introduce positional error.
HM Land Registry warns that conversion from British National Grid to WGS84 may shift some features by up to 15 metres.
Keeping the original British National Grid geometry avoids introducing an unnecessary web-map reprojection step into parcel matching.
guards: Retain EPSG:27700 source geometry for authoritative candidate matching and record any reprojection separately.
Do not compare reprojected web-map geometry to metre/sub-metre acceptance thresholds without transformation provenance.
Reject any workflow that silently treats WGS84/web-map coordinates as identical to British National Grid coordinates.

facts: The title plan and register cannot describe the land more accurately than the pre-registration deeds allow.
A plan lodged for registration or search must allow the land to be identified clearly on the Ordnance Survey map.
If land cannot be clearly identified on the Ordnance Survey map, an application may be rejected, requisitioned or cancelled.
Where an approved estate plan exists, a transfer or lease plan must be based on the current approved version.
A verbal reference to plot numbers on an approved estate plan is not accepted as a substitute for the required plan.
If the seller's or landlord's title plan does not clearly define the transferred extent, a plan must be prepared.
For unusual extents such as airspace or subsoil, HM Land Registry needs the depth or height specifically included or excluded.
Ordnance Survey Datum can be used to define height to fine tolerances.
Plans and property descriptions should reflect the current state of the property and must not contradict each other.
guards: Do not promote a parcel candidate whose plan cannot be confidently related to current OS mapping.
Do not let a newer geometric source silently override contradictory deed/register evidence.
Require explicit vertical-reference evidence for airspace, subsoil or level-based height candidates.

facts: Preferred deed-plan scales are 1:1250 to 1:500 for urban property and 1:2500 for rural property.
A plan should show its orientation, for example with a north point.
A plan should be based on metric measurement.
A plan should include a bar scale.
A plan should ideally not be marked 'for identification only' or equivalent wording.
A plan should not be endorsed 'Do not scale from this drawing' or equivalent disclaimer wording.
Undefined boundaries should be shown accurately and, where necessary, by reference to measurements.
Measurements should correspond, so far as possible, with scaled measurements.
Measurements should be expressed in metres to two decimal places.
guards: Reject candidate geometry derived from a plan whose effective scale is unknown or contradicted by printing/copying.
Do not use disclaimer-marked drawings as precision boundary evidence without stronger corroboration.
Store stated scale, bar-scale presence, orientation and measurement units as separate evidence fields.

facts: HM Land Registry lists missing deed plans among defects that may cause rejection.
Unsigned plans can be defective where signatures are required.
A scale that makes the land extent uncertain can make a plan unacceptable.
A reduced plan that still carries the original scale endorsement can be defective unless an effective bar scale or corrected scale is provided.
Plans marked 'for identification only' may be rejected if the extent cannot otherwise be related accurately.
Omitted colour or marking references can make the depicted extent incomplete.
Unclear easement extent can make a plan deficient.
Plans that cannot be confidently located or oriented against the Ordnance Survey map can be rejected.
Photocopying and PDF printing can distort plans or reduce clarity and scale.
guards: Do not promote copied/scanned plan geometry without checking distortion and effective scale.
Reject ambiguous thick edging where it obscures the boundary or underlying detail.
Record whether geometry came from an original, official copy, photocopy, scan or printed PDF.

facts: HM Land Registry's title-plan guidance was updated on 13 July 2026.
A title plan must be viewed together with the register and referenced filed documents.
The title plan supports the property description by showing the general extent of registered land.
All title plans show general boundaries unless a boundary is recorded as determined under section 60 of the Land Registration Act 2002.
Title plans may be vector, raster or older drawer/canister plans.
Newly created title plans are vector plans.
Title plans are usually 1:1250 in urban areas and 1:2500 in rural areas, with 1:5000 or 1:10000 possible for large rural extents.
HM Land Registry does not routinely survey land where deed plans and OS mapping are compatible.
Undefined boundaries may be plotted with pecked lines where the property is not fully defined by physical OS features.
guards: Do not infer exact legal boundary position from ordinary title-plan red edging.
Require register/deed context before using title-plan references as candidate evidence.
Preserve title-plan type and scale because raster/legacy and vector evidence have different extraction risks.

facts: Measurements shown on title plans originate from title-deed plans and provide only an additional indication of boundary position.
A title plan showing measurements still shows only the general boundary unless a determined boundary applies.
Reference points or features used for old dimensions may have disappeared or changed.
Dimensions from deed plans are no longer routinely reproduced on title plans.
HM Land Registry receives Ordnance Survey map updates daily but title plans are not routinely updated.
A title plan can remain in its original form until title activity triggers an update.
Replacement title plans may be prepared where latest survey information must be considered.
A small percentage of registration applications or enquiries prompt a survey.
Surveys may be used to check existing mapped detail, obtain ground measurements and record the nature of boundary features.
guards: Do not treat an old dimension on a title plan as current exact survey control without verifying its reference features.
Record title-plan date/version separately from current OS mapping or LiDAR survey date.
Do not infer that lack of a recent title-plan update means the underlying OS mapping or occupation has not changed.

facts: Environment Agency Time Stamped Point Cloud is an archive of three-dimensional x, y and z LiDAR points and attributes.
Site-specific Environment Agency LiDAR surveys across England date back to 1998, with point-cloud availability going back to 2006.
There may not be a matching point cloud for every time-stamped DSM or DTM because of historic archiving.
Point-cloud processing classifies returns into ground and surface-object classes.
Manual editing of the derived DTM means classified ground points do not necessarily match the final DTM.
Point-cloud data is distributed in 5km download zip files by survey year.
LAZ files are aligned to the Ordnance Survey grid.
Coverage metadata provides survey flight start and end dates.
Coverage metadata can provide additional attributes such as average point density.
guards: Do not substitute point-cloud ground points for the final edited DTM without explicitly recording the product change.
Require survey-date and tile metadata before comparing LiDAR elevations across time.
Do not assume a point-cloud tile exists merely because a corresponding DTM/DSM tile exists.

facts: Environment Agency Composite DTM covers about 99% of England at 1m spatial resolution.
The Composite DTM is terrain-only data produced by removing surface objects from the DSM.
Composite DTM tiles are GeoTIFF rasters aligned to the OS National Grid and elevations are in metres referenced to Ordnance Datum Newlyn.
The Composite DTM uses the OSTN15 transformation method.
Individual LiDAR surveys contributing to the Composite DTM have vertical accuracy of +/-15cm RMSE.
OS Net base-station coordinate standard errors are generally better than 0.008m in plan and 0.020m in height.
OSTN15 defines the OSGB36 National Grid in conjunction with OS Net stations.
OSGM15 mainland Great Britain height standard error is about 0.008m, excluding GNSS heighting errors.
Ordnance Survey notes that transformation/model accuracy must be separated from GNSS observation error and from mapping/product accuracy.
guards: Keep LiDAR vertical RMSE, OSGM15 model error and boundary-position uncertainty as separate error-budget components.
Do not present coordinate or raster decimal precision as a substitute for documented survey accuracy.
Do not promote a height-difference row unless horizontal CRS, vertical datum, survey provenance and boundary evidence are all explicit.
